title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 11.4.1 Writing: Mechanics of Writing (Spelling)

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Some English words are easy to misspell because the letters do not match the sounds one by one. In this sub-strand you will spot common mistakes in sports words and everyday words, learn patterns that help, and write the words correctly in sentences.

## Strand 11.0: Sports: My Favourite Game
Sub-strand 11.4.1: Writing: Mechanics of Writing (Spelling)
Suggested lessons: 2

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify commonly misspelt words in oral and written contexts
b) write commonly misspelt words correctly for communication clarity
c) adopt the skill of writing words clearly and correctly in communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Commonly Misspelt Words

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why is it difficult to spell some words correctly?
2. How can we become better at spelling words?

## Core competencies
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: This is nurtured as the learner makes words from jumbled up letters.
• Learning to learn: This is enhanced as the learner learns how to spell commonly misspelt words through learner centred- activities.

## Values
• Responsibility is encouraged as the learner engages in assigned roles of searching for commonly misspelt words and creating puzzles.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Effective Communication: The learner learns how to spell words correctly and can therefore communicate by writing effectively.
• Self-esteem is developed as the learner engages in games-related activities such as creating a puzzle with commonly misspelt words.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to apply knowledge on proper spelling skills to all learning areas as they all insist on correct spelling.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 11.0 Sports: My Favourite Game, Sub-strand 11.4.1 Mechanics of Writing: Spelling

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Words that are often misspelt

LESSON 1: WORDS THAT ARE OFTEN MISSPELT
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Recognise common spelling mistakes in speech and writing.
• Explain why some words are hard to spell.
• Use a personal list of words to watch.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify commonly misspelt words in oral and written contexts

## Introduction
You can say friend clearly and still write frind. Spelling is not the same job as speaking. The letters have to be right even when a sound is silent or when two words sound alike.

## Notes
### Why some spellings are hard
English spelling grew over a long time, so a sound may be written in more than one way. Some words keep letters we hardly hear, such as the t in whistle. Some pairs sound alike but mean different things, such as their and there. If you write the wrong one, the sentence changes its meaning.

### A list to learn
Say each word, spell it aloud, then cover it and write it.

- because: be + cause. Not becouse and not becaus.
- friend: the vowel letters are i then e. A friend stands by you to the end.
- favourite: keep our in the middle. Fav-our-ite.
- receive: after the letter c, write ei. You receive a pass.
- separate: there is a rat in separate: sep-a-rat-e.
- tomorrow: one m, then double r. To-mor-row.
- their: belongs to them. Their kit is clean.
- there: a place. The ball is over there. They're means they are, and it needs an apostrophe.
- lose: you lose a match when you do not win. Loose means not tight. A loose lace is dangerous.
- practice: the noun, a thing. We have football practice.
- practise: the verb, an action. We practise every Thursday. (In the English used in Kenyan schools, the verb has an s.)
- referee: re-fe-ree. It ends with double e.
- athletics: ath-let-ics. Do not add an extra e after th.
- whistle: whis-tle. The t is silent, but it must be written.
- exercise, competition, captain: ex-er-cise, com-pe-ti-tion, cap-tain.

### Spotting a mistake
Read this sentence from a sports report and find the errors: 'Tommorow our freind will recieve the whistle becouse she is the captian.'

The intended words are tomorrow, friend, receive, because and captain. Hearing the sentence is not enough. You have to see the letters.

Keep a page in your vocabulary book for words you miss. Write the wrong try, cross it out, and write the correct spelling beside it three times.

## Key words
• misspelt — written with the wrong letters
• apostrophe — the sign ' used in they're to show that a letter has been left out
• noun — a word that names a person, place, thing or idea
• verb — a word that tells what someone does or is

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which spelling is correct, and why: recieve or receive?

Working:
1. Look at the letter before the vowel pair.
2. After c, the pattern is ei.

Answer: receive. After c we write ei.

### Example 2
Choose their or there: The players left ______ bags over ______.

Working:
1. Bags belonging to them need their.
2. A place needs there.

Answer: The players left their bags over there.

## Activity: Dictation and a puzzle list
You will need: Vocabulary book, Cards or squared paper
1. Listen to ten words from the list and write them as a dictation. Do not shout the spelling while others write.
2. Mark your work with the list in the notes. Circle any word you missed.
3. With a partner, search your old exercise books for two more words you often misspell and add them to your list.
4. Turn four correct spellings into a simple word search or jumbled-letter puzzle for another pair.

## Practice
1. Rewrite correctly: becouse, freind, tommorow, recieve.
2. What is the difference between lose and loose?
3. Why is whistle easy to misspell?
4. Fill the gaps with their or there: ______ coach is standing over ______.

## Summary
• Some words are hard because of silent letters or because two words sound alike.
• Learn because, friend, favourite, receive, separate, tomorrow, their, there, lose and loose.
• Keep a list of your own mistakes and correct them.

### Answers to practice
1. because, friend, tomorrow, receive
2. Lose means not to win or to be unable to find something. Loose means not tight.
3. The t is silent, so writers sometimes leave it out.
4. Their coach is standing over there.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Writing the words correctly

LESSON 2: WRITING THE WORDS CORRECTLY
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Spell the target words correctly from memory.
• Use them in sentences about sport.
• Build a habit of checking spelling before you hand in work.

Curriculum outcomes: b) write commonly misspelt words correctly for communication clarity; c) adopt the skill of writing words clearly and correctly in communication

## Introduction
A puzzle is useful only if the letters end in the real word. Jumbling referee is a game. Leaving it jumbled in a composition is a mistake a reader has to solve.

## Notes
### From jumbled letters to words
Rearrange each set, then say the word.

- eeferre → referee
- sletichta → athletics
- eltsihw → whistle
- etiruovaf → favourite
- esuaceb → because
- etarapes → separate
- ecitcarp → practice
- esitcarp → practise

Check the number of letters. Athletics has nine letters. Referee has seven. If your answer is short, a letter is still missing.

### Sentences that show the meaning
A correct spelling should also sit in a true sentence.

- The referee blew the whistle to start the match.
- Athletics practice is tomorrow on the field.
- We practise our passes because the competition is soon.
- My favourite game is separate from my homework time, but both matter.
- Do not lose your bottle, and tie a loose lace before you run.
- Their captain will receive the prize over there.

Notice practise in 'We practise' because it is a verb, and practice in 'Athletics practice' because it names the session.

### A checking habit
Before you give in any written work, pause at words you know are tricky. Spell them in your head or look at your list. Write slowly enough for every letter. Clear, correct words let a coach, a teacher or a friend read your meaning at once. That is why spelling is part of communication, not an extra decoration.

If you are unsure, write the word two ways on a scrap of paper and choose the one that matches your list. Guessing in the middle of a neat sentence often leaves the wrong try behind.

## Key words
• jumbled — mixed up, not in the right order
• competition — an event in which people or teams try to win
• habit — something you do regularly, almost without being reminded

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Unjumble sletichta and use the word in a sentence.

Working:
1. Count nine letters: a-t-h-l-e-t-i-c-s.
2. The word names running, jumping and throwing sports.

Answer: athletics. Example: Our class enjoys athletics on Friday.

### Example 2
Choose practice or practise: The team will ______ after school. Evening ______ is at four.

Working:
1. The first gap is an action, so it needs the verb practise.
2. The second gap names the session, so it needs the noun practice.

Answer: The team will practise after school. Evening practice is at four.

## Activity: Peer dictation
You will need: Vocabulary books, Scrap paper, The word list
1. In pairs, one learner dictates five sentences that use words from the list. Speak clearly and do not spell the words unless your partner asks after the whole sentence.
2. The partner writes the sentences, then you swap roles.
3. Mark the spellings together against the list.
4. Copy every corrected word once into your vocabulary book and write one new sentence of your own.

## Practice
1. Unjumble and write the word: eeferre.
2. Write a sentence using favourite and because.
3. Correct the sentence: Tommorow we will loose the race if we do not practice.
4. Why does correct spelling help communication?

## Summary
• Unjumble letters carefully and count them.
• Use practise for the action and practice for the session.
• Check tricky words before you hand in your writing.

### Answers to practice
1. referee
2. Example: Football is my favourite game because I like to pass and score.
3. Tomorrow we will lose the race if we do not practise.
4. The reader understands your meaning at once and is not stopped by the wrong word.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 11.4.1 WRITING: MECHANICS OF WRITING (SPELLING)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which spelling is correct?
   A. becouse
   B. because
   C. becaus
   D. becauze

2. Which spelling is correct?
   A. recieve
   B. receive
   C. receeve
   D. recive

3. The ball is over ______. Their or there?
   A. their
   B. there
   C. they're
   D. thier

4. Which word means not tight?
   A. lose
   B. loose
   C. loss
   D. lost

5. Choose the correct sentence.
   A. We practise on Thursday.
   B. We practize on Thursday.
   C. We practce on Thursday.
   D. We praktise on Thursday.

6. Which is the correct spelling of the person who controls a match?
   A. referree
   B. referee
   C. refree
   D. refferee

7. Unjumble eltsihw.
   A. whistle
   B. whistel
   C. wistle
   D. whissle

8. Athletics is correctly spelt as
   A. atheletics
   B. athletics
   C. athlethics
   D. athlatics

9. Tomorrow our friend will receive the prize. Which words in that sentence are often misspelt?

10. Why should you check spelling before you hand in work?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 11.4.1 WRITING: MECHANICS OF WRITING (SPELLING)
========================================

1. B. because
   Because is be + cause.

2. B. receive
   After c, write ei: receive.

3. B. there
   There names a place. Their shows belonging.

4. B. loose
   Loose means not tight. Lose means not to win.

5. A. We practise on Thursday.
   The verb in school English is practise.

6. B. referee
   Referee has one f and ends with ee.

7. A. whistle
   Whistle keeps a silent t.

8. B. athletics
   Athletics is ath-let-ics, with no extra e after ath.

9. Tomorrow, friend and receive.
   Writers often add an extra m, swap ie, or write ei in the wrong order.

10. Correct spelling makes the writing clear so the reader understands you at once.
   Spelling is part of clear written communication.
